name: Tomas Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer order-change calls at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and took this job after years of delivery driving; I know streets better than I know the centre’s refund screen. I am still learning and earn the usual agent rate. I use the approved AI search every day to find a delivery rule, then check the order number before I tell anyone what it says.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ruth sells bread at a small shop, and our children are grown and have left home. We have about four months of expenses saved, with some other centres in reach. I take pride in showing up for a shift and getting the order right. Retirement is near enough to discuss at dinner, but I have not checked an amount that would let us set a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AI Plateau sounds like the rule search we already have, only quicker. I would still ask for the original order number before changing a delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I will keep getting my normal shifts. Four months saved takes the edge off a broken appliance, and there are some other desks nearby if this one changes slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep doing order-change calls and check each AI search result against the delivery address. In the first year of this small change, I’d show a new agent how to spot an old address in a current order during a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A quick answer is fine if the parcel still reaches the right door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which address was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a customer had moved, and the search brought up the previous delivery address. I read the current order aloud before changing the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth (my partner) and I would leave our four-month reserve alone. It is there for bills when work stops unexpectedly, not to buy a new device.

say: I’d say **AI search** speeds up rule finding but needs an order check.
I’d teach agents to confirm **current addresses** before changing deliveries.
think: I think my **normal shifts** continue under small changes.
I trust our **four-month reserve** for an ordinary setback.
do: Keep **order-change calls** and check AI search against current delivery addresses.
Show a new agent **old-address mistakes** during a paid shift.
feel: **Calm** about wages and the mild tool change.
S0.quote: A quick answer is fine if the parcel still reaches the right door.
fieldNote: He brings **delivery-driver experience** but remains junior on refund screens.
His **daily AI use** is checked against current orders.
The **four-month reserve** is retained, not a new savings pledge.

steps.text: Keep handling order changes and checking AI results against current addresses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will handle basic delivery changes and leave us the ones where a package is already moving. I would ask for a paid hour to learn the new routing assistant before judging it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can pick up that tool, but a junior on the ordinary queue may still lose shifts. My old driving knowledge helps me spot a bad route; it does not make the centre pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take the centre’s paid routing-assistant lesson and use it on three live cases with an experienced agent beside me. In the first year basic changes move, I’d ask for the paid rota and apply for a posted paid returns-counter job if the written weekly wage and hours cover our bills after travel; I’d keep this job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, curious about the route map. I want to see the parcel on a road before I trust a green tick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a parcel marked “rerouted” after it had already left the depot. A promise to change the van at that point can make an agent look foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a counter offer compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth (my partner) would compare the counter’s closing time with the last bus. I would not trade a full call week for three attractive shifts.

say: I’d ask for a **paid routing lesson** before judging the new assistant.
I’d challenge a **reroute promise** after a parcel leaves the depot.
think: I think my **driving knowledge** helps me catch bad routes.
I fear **junior hours** could still shrink on the basic queue.
do: Learn **routing assistant** during a paid lesson and three supervised live cases in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid returns-counter work** if written weekly pay/hours cover bills after travel and last bus; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, curious about the route map.
S1.quote: I want to see the parcel on a road before I trust a green tick.
fieldNote: His **new AI lesson** includes supervised live use, beyond existing rule search.
He requests a **paid rota** himself, not with a worker group.
The counter must provide **full-week pay** and a last bus home.

steps.text: Learn routing assistant through paid lesson and three supervised live cases
Apply for posted paid counter with written bill-covering net pay/hours, last bus; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers AGI by 2028 could change an order and speak to its customer without us. Robots around 2031 are later, so the first cut could come to the phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior call wage could go quickly. Four months saved gives Ruth and me time to inspect an opening, but the bread-shop wage alone will not carry our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d put our planned replacement freezer on hold while the old one still works, and check posted paid parcel-counter openings near the bus route. If calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only after a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after travel; I’d keep my present shifts until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but still able to choose among a few openings. A working freezer can wait longer than the next wage packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a counter worker handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the counter receives actual returned parcels or only types their numbers into another screen. The first sounds like work I know, though robots around 2031 might reach it later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the freezer plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth (my partner) and I would compare the bus fare with the whole week of pay. We will not leave a paying shift on a manager’s friendly nod.

say: I’d warn **2028 AGI** could take customer calls before robots.
I’d ask whether **paid counter openings** actually exist nearby.
think: I think my **junior wage** could end quickly.
I know **four months saved** gives only a limited search.
do: Defer the **freezer replacement** while it works and inspect posted paid counters in 2026.
Move after call loss only on **signed written offer** with weekly pay and hours covering bills after travel.
feel: **Alarmed** about a quick wage loss, with options to inspect.
S2.quote: A working freezer can wait longer than the next wage packet.
fieldNote: The **freezer delay** is conditional on the current appliance working.
He considers **physical returns**, while knowing robots could later reach that work.
The signed offer must cover **whole-week pay after fare**.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid parcel-counter openings near bus routes
Move after call loss only on signed written weekly pay/hours covering bills after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to watch a counter worker take a real return and see whether the job still pays. I would not sign up for a course just because a poster promises future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my delivery years could help me sort wrong-address returns, even if AI reads the order record. Robots around 2034 might change handling later, and I do not pretend a counter is permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask a local shop for a supervised paid return-counter shift only if it has a posted paid vacancy. In the first year after 2031, I’d take that job only if a signed offer shows written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after fare; I’d keep my current call wage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a five-year window gives me a chance to inspect the till and the parcels. I would rather have one paid shift than a training badge with no opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a counter shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would weigh a damaged return, record its order number and ask the experienced worker where it goes. If I only forward a photograph, I have not found a new kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you both reach work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth (my partner) would check the closing shift against the bus and her early bakery start. We need both work journeys to fit before I accept.

say: I’d seek a **supervised paid counter shift** for a posted opening.
I’d reject a **course advert** without paid work behind it.
think: I think my **delivery experience** could help with returns.
I know **2034 robots** may later change physical parcel handling.
do: Try **supervised paid return work** only for a posted vacancy in 2026.
Take **posted counter job** after 2031 only with signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages, hours and both commutes.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to inspect paid counter work.
S3.quote: I would rather have one paid shift than a training badge with no opening.
fieldNote: He seeks **paid observation** tied to a real vacancy, without promising a course.
His **delivery background** may help physical returns but not guarantee work.
The **two commutes** and full-week pay gate a move.

steps.text: Try supervised paid return-counter shift only for posted paid vacancy
Take counter job only on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages, hours and both commutes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AGI by 2036 gives us years to see whether anyone still pays for order calls. I would ask for the actual rota each spring, not a retirement speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may have stopped working by 68, but I have not checked what Ruth and I could live on, so I cannot promise that. Full thinking AI could still reach the calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 would come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid order calls and ask Ruth to sit with me over our bills and any verified income for later life. If I still need wages after 2036 and the calls fall, I’d look for posted paid work I can reach and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end, steady enough to use the years. I would rather make a plan from a pay slip than from my birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the page?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check what income is really available before deciding whether to stop. Our four-month reserve is useful, but it does not tell me what comes in every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children be involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children might have suggestions, and I would listen if they offered. I would not put their money on our page unless they offered it and we understood the limits.

say: I’d ask for **actual spring rotas** instead of a retirement speech.
I’d tell coworkers **2036 AI** may still reach order calls.
think: I think I **might stop work** by 68, if real income allows it.
I cannot assume **retirement pay** without checking the amount.
do: Keep **paid order calls** and review bills with Ruth against verified later-life income.
Seek **posted paid work** if wages still needed and calls fall; move only on signed written weekly pay/hours covering bills after travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036, steadier with time to check.
S4.quote: I would rather make a plan from a pay slip than from my birthday.
fieldNote: He treats **retirement timing** as contingent on verified income.
The **four-month reserve** does not substitute for a monthly wage.
Children’s **help remains uncertain** and outside the budget.

steps.text: Keep paid order calls and review bills against verified later-life income with Ruth
Seek reachable posted paid work if wages needed/calls fall; move on signed written bill-covering net pay/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the plain order changes I handle could disappear before I become good at the complicated ones. Four months saved gives us room to look, but not a wage for life. I would want early written notice and a real paid counter opening with enough weekly hours to cover our bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I used to drive parcels to the right door. If a new job pays me to check a real parcel, I would rather try that than buy a promise about a future office title.

headlineQuote: If a new job pays me to check a real parcel, I would rather try that than buy a promise about a future office title.
portrait: At **58**, Tomas is a junior order agent still learning after secondary school and years of delivery driving.
He and Ruth have **grown children**, typical pay and about four months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI search daily** but checks order numbers against original records.
He values **practical paid work** and local counter openings over speculative study.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove plain order changes before he masters harder calls.
whatWouldHelp: **Early written notice** and a real paid counter opening with enough weekly hours would help.
